questions.question: A muddy river pours into a calm lake. Bits of rock, sand, mud and broken shell sink and settle on the lake's floor, one layer on top of another, a little more every year. What is this loose, settled material called?
choices: Sediment
Bedrock
Magma
Humus
questions.context: Sediment is the loose bits of rock, sand, mud and shell that water, wind or ice carry along and drop somewhere else, where they pile up in layers. Bedrock is the solid rock under the ground, magma is melted rock deep underground, and humus is rotted plant and animal matter in soil.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.10B has 5th graders model how sedimentary rock forms, starting from bits of rock, sand, mud and shells that settle in layers in lakes and oceans.

questions.question: Loose grains of sand and mud can become solid rock, such as sandstone and shale, but only over a very long time. What turns the loose grains into rock?
questions.answer: They are pressed together and glued by minerals
choices: They are pressed together and glued by minerals
They are dried out and baked hard by the Sun
They are melted together by heat deep underground
They are frozen together by ice in cold winters
questions.context: The weight of the layers above presses the grains below tightly together and squeezes out the water. Minerals carried in the water between the grains then glue them together, the way cement holds a sidewalk together. This takes thousands to millions of years; mud that only dries in the Sun has not become rock.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.10B asks 5th graders to describe how sedimentary rock forms: layers pressed down by the weight above them and stuck together by minerals.

questions.question: On a warm, shallow sea floor, the shells and skeletons of countless sea creatures pile up, mixed with broken bits of coral. Over a very long time they become rock. Which rock forms this way?
choices: Limestone
Sandstone
Shale
Coal
questions.context: Limestone is made mostly of calcite, the hard material of shells, corals and skeletons, and it is often full of fossil shells. Sandstone forms from sand, shale from mud, and coal from the plants of ancient swamps.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.10B lessons name sandstone, shale and limestone as the sedimentary rocks 5th graders meet, with limestone as shells and ocean bits turned to rock.

questions.question: Most living things that die never become fossils. A fish dies in a lake long ago. What gives its bones the best chance of becoming one?
questions.answer: Mud and sand bury it quickly
choices: Mud and sand bury it quickly
It lies uncovered for many years
Scavengers pick its bones clean
Waves wash it up onto the shore
questions.context: Mud and sand that cover a body quickly keep scavengers away and slow its rotting, so the hard bones last long enough to be preserved. A body left in the open is eaten or rots away, which is why very few living things ever become fossils.
questions.grade_note: Elementary fossil lessons teach that very few living things become fossils and that the remains must be buried quickly in sediment (Bridgewater State lesson); fifth-grade units teach how fossils are preserved (Math/Science Nucleus Fifth Grade Past Life).

questions.question: Fossil hunters find fossils again and again in sandstone and shale, but almost never in rock that formed from lava. Why does lava rock hold so few fossils?
questions.answer: Lava's heat destroys dead plants and animals
choices: Lava's heat destroys dead plants and animals
No plants or animals lived near volcanoes
Lava rock formed before life on Earth began
Lava rock is too hard for fossils to form in
questions.context: Melted rock is so hot that it wipes away the remains of living things. Sandstone, shale and limestone are sedimentary rocks, built from layers of sediment that bury remains gently, without that heat, so most fossils are found in them.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.10B lessons teach that fossils are almost always found in sedimentary rock, and 'fossils can be found in any rock' is a misconception they correct.

questions.question: A fossil hunter splits a slab of shale and finds the shape of a fern leaf pressed into the rock. Nothing of the leaf itself is left, only its print. Does the print count as a fossil?
questions.answer: Yes, because it is a print left by a living thing
choices: Yes, because it is a print left by a living thing
Yes, because any shape found inside a rock is a fossil
No, because a fossil must be a bone, a tooth or a shell
No, because a fossil must be a piece of the living thing
questions.context: A fossil is any preserved remains, print or trace of a living thing from long ago, usually more than 10,000 years old. Leaf prints, footprints and burrows are fossils just as bones and shells are, but a shape that no living thing made is not.
questions.grade_note: Grade 3-5 fossil lessons (the National Park Service's) teach impression fossils, and the idea that a fossil must be a bone is a misconception these grades are taught out of.

questions.question: A farmer ploughing a dry wheat field turns up rocks full of fossil corals and starfish. What do these fossils show about the field long ago?
choices: An ocean once covered it
A lake once covered it
A river once ran across it
A glacier once covered it
questions.context: Corals and starfish live only in the sea, never in lakes or rivers, so their fossils mean seawater once covered this land. Fossils like these tell scientists what a place was like long ago.
questions.grade_note: Fossils as clues to past environments, such as sea fossils found on dry land, are taught in grades 3-5 (NGSS 3-LS4-1, 4-ESS1-1) and are part of the 5th-grade fossil line G5.E4 builds on.

questions.question: A tiny insect, wings and all, lies sealed inside a lump of clear, golden amber that is millions of years old. What was the amber when the insect was trapped in it?
questions.answer: Sticky resin oozing from a tree
choices: Sticky resin oozing from a tree
Sticky honey dripping from a hive
Soft mud at the edge of a pond
Thick tar seeping from the ground
questions.context: Amber is tree resin, a sticky gum that oozes from some trees; many books call it sap. An insect stuck in fresh resin was sealed in, and over millions of years the buried resin hardened into amber with the insect still inside.
questions.grade_note: Fifth-grade fossil units teach how fossils are preserved, and an insect in amber is one of their pictured examples (Math/Science Nucleus Fifth Grade Past Life).

questions.question: Oil is pumped up from rock deep underground. It formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient life, buried and slowly cooked by heat and pressure. What did most oil form from?
questions.answer: Tiny living things adrift in the sea
choices: Tiny living things adrift in the sea
Dinosaurs that roamed across the land
Trees that grew in swampy forests
Whales that swam in the open ocean
questions.context: Most oil formed from trillions of tiny algae and plankton that sank to the sea floor and were buried in mud; natural gas often forms alongside it. Oil from dinosaurs is a myth, and coal, not oil, formed mostly from the plants of ancient swamps.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.10B has 5th graders describe how fossil fuels formed, with oil and natural gas mainly from tiny ocean life (plankton), and corrects the idea that oil comes from dinosaurs.
